subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 7 periods = 350 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 5h 50min

periods.section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
periods.activity_title: Riddles, Roles, and Reading the Poem Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.57): four riddles identifying vocations — farmer, potter, mason, cook
Reflect and Respond (p.57): class discussion on the social role of identified vocations

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes the poem (pp.57–60) and reads the four riddles from Reflect and Respond aloud. Students respond briefly to each riddle in their notebooks, identifying the vocation in one word.

Class discussion on Reflect and Respond: students share answers and explore how each identified vocation — farmer, potter, mason, cook — contributes to society. Teacher builds a quick chalkboard web of occupations and their community value.

Teacher reads the full poem aloud, students following in their textbooks (pp.57–60). Teacher models a slow, reverential pace to reflect the poem's celebratory tone. A second read is done with volunteer students taking one vocation-line each, rehearsing the auditory quality of the verse.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's opening riddles are a warm-up for the vocations the poem celebrates — draw students into the idea that ordinary work carries dignity before the poem makes that claim explicitly. The circular structure (the poem's identical first and last lines) is worth pointing to during the read-aloud but not analysed here — it will be handled when the appreciation tasks are reached.
materials: Chalkboard or whiteboard for vocation web

periods.section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
periods.activity_title: Appreciating Free Verse: Structure, Speaker, Tone, and Mood

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.60): rhyme scheme, lineation, and line-pattern analysis
Reading for Appreciation (p.60): speaker identification and her/his role in the poem
Reading for Appreciation (p.60–61): fill-in-the-blanks on tone and mood from the given word box

time_bands.activity: Brief re-reading of the poem by the class (students read silently, pp.57–60). Teacher prompts: notice whether any two lines rhyme and whether line lengths are uniform — record first impressions.

Teacher leads analysis of Reading for Appreciation — Rhyme Scheme and Lineation (p.60): does the poem rhyme? What is the effect of varying line lengths? What pattern structures most lines? Students answer in pairs then share with the class.
Class discussion on the Speaker task (p.60): who is the 'I' in the poem and what is that voice's role — observer, celebrant, witness? Students justify with lines from the poem.

Students complete the Tone and Mood fill-in-the-blanks (pp.60–61) individually using the given word box: reverential, celebratory, joyful. Class shares answers; teacher consolidates on the board, distinguishing tone (the poet's attitude) from mood (the reader's feeling).

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the poem read aloud, students are ready to move from impressions to formal analysis. The three tasks here address form (free verse), voice (the speaker-witness), and affect (tone/mood) — keep them in that order so structure is established before feeling is named. A common difficulty is confusing the poet with the speaker; press students to say what the text shows, not what they assume about the author.

periods.section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
periods.activity_title: Imagery, Metaphor, Personification, Repetition, Alliteration, Symbolism

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.61): visual and auditory imagery — select descriptions, fill auditory blanks
Reading for Appreciation (p.61): metaphor — true/false on 'delicious singing of the cook'
Reading for Appreciation (p.61): personification — identify the line attributing human qualities to vocations
Reading for Appreciation (p.61): repetition — why the poem begins and ends with the same line
Reading for Appreciation (p.61): alliteration — identify two examples from the poem
Reading for Appreciation (p.61): symbolism — what each vocation symbolises beyond a job

time_bands.activity: Teacher works through the Imagery task (p.61) with the class: students first select two visual descriptions, then fill in the blanks for auditory imagery (artisans with lutes, the cook's singing, the electricians humming). Discussion focuses on how sensory detail makes each vocation vivid.

Students answer the metaphor true/false on 'delicious singing' (p.61) and the personification task (p.61) individually. Pairs compare responses; teacher brings out how 'celebrating' and 'humming' give vocations human agency, and how 'delicious' crosses from taste to sound.

Class works through repetition, alliteration, and symbolism (p.61) in a teacher-led discussion. For repetition, students articulate the circular structure's effect; for alliteration, they locate examples (e.g. 'cables and cables', 'sailing and singing'); for symbolism, they argue what each vocation stands for beyond occupation — identity, pride, cultural heritage.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the densest in the appreciation sequence and covers six devices. Moving briskly through metaphor and personification (both accessible) will protect time for symbolism, which demands the most analytical lift at secondary level. Students often identify alliteration mechanically — push them to explain its sonic effect in context.
materials: Chalkboard for device labels and examples

periods.section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
periods.activity_title: True/False Comprehension and Critical Reflection Extract

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.60): seven true/false statements with rectification of false ones
Critical Reflection I (p.62): extract on shoemakers and cook — MCQ, SCR, symbolism, phrase identification, fill-in

time_bands.activity: Students complete the seven true/false statements from Check Your Understanding (p.60) individually in notebooks. After individual work, teacher reads each statement aloud; students raise hands for true/false and volunteers correct false statements with the exact line from the poem.

Students locate the Critical Reflection I extract (p.62: shoemakers and cook lines) in their textbooks and work through all five sub-questions: meaning of 'affirm', what quality shoes enable, what 'return home' symbolises, the phrase showing each worker's contribution is distinct, and the fill-in completion. Teacher circulates, then takes class feedback on each sub-question, building answers on the board. Focus especially on the symbolism sub-question — 'return home' as safety, completion of the day's dignified work.

periods.teacher_notes: Having completed the appreciation sequence, students now apply comprehension at two levels: factual recall (Check Your Understanding) and analytical extract work (Critical Reflection I). A common error is treating 'return home' as only literal — press students to articulate what the feet doing all those activities represent in the poem's world.

periods.section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection Discussion and Vocation Vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection II (p.62–63): six extended-answer questions on identity, imagery, sensory language
Vocabulary in Context (p.63): match six vocation terms — horticulturist, ASHA worker, sericulturist, confectioner, goldsmith, welder

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.64): identify non-synonyms for myriad, hues, precision, varied, delicious

time_bands.activity: Teacher guides class discussion on Critical Reflection II (pp.62–63): all six questions taken in sequence. Students respond orally in full sentences — teacher probes for textual evidence on questions about 'I hear Bharat celebrating', the electrician humming, and the line 'The voice of their vocation is the voice of their identity.' Students draft brief written answers for the two longer evaluation questions.

Vocabulary in Context matching task (p.63): students individually match the six vocation terms (horticulturist, ASHA worker, sericulturist, confectioner, goldsmith, welder) to their descriptions. Class verification follows; teacher explains etymology or root meanings where time allows — 'horticultural', 'sericulture', 'goldsmith craft traditions'.

periods.teacher_notes: Critical Reflection II is the analytical centrepiece of the poem's reading spine — the six questions move from the speaker's intent to the poem's use of sensory imagery and connect explicitly to the poem's Whitman inspiration. The vocabulary matching task extends the poem's theme (vocations celebrated in the poem) into six additional occupations, keeping the conceptual frame intact.

periods.section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
periods.activity_title: Listening to Occupations and Speaking as a Vocation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond I (p.64): two-to-three-word answer on what the boy uses to understand his father's tools
Listen and Respond II (p.64–65): four MCQ questions on the conversation about parents' occupations
Speaking Activity (p.64): groups of five, each student speaks on an assigned vocation from the poem for one to two minutes

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the listening context: students will hear a conversation between two friends discussing their parents' occupations — one mother works as a line supervisor at a spare-parts factory, one father is an automobile mechanic. Students prepare to answer in two to three words only for the first listen.

Teacher reads (or plays) the transcript from Appendix (p.262) twice. First pass: students note the two-to-three-word answer to Listen and Respond I (what the boy uses to understand tools). Second pass: students answer the four multiple-choice questions from Listen and Respond II (pp.64–65). Class verification of all answers follows.

Speaking Activity (p.64): teacher forms groups of five and allots one poem-vocation per student — carpenter, boatman, shoemaker, electrician, cook. Each student speaks for one to two minutes adopting that vocation's voice: who they are, what they do, a problem they face, and a message for all. Peers listen for the connection between the spoken identity and the poem's line about that vocation.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript grounds the poem's celebration of vocations in a contemporary, conversational register — the boy's mechanical-manual reading habit is a real-world echo of the poem's 'carpenters with mathematical precision.' For the speaking activity, remind students to keep their vocation's poem line in mind as an anchor for their monologue, but not to reproduce it verbatim.

periods.section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
periods.activity_title: Poster Writing, Haiku, and Comparative Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.64): complete the Career Mela poster — fields for organiser, purpose, date, highlights, slogan, entry, sponsors
Learning Beyond the Text (p.67–68): compose a Haiku poem celebrating a vocation using the 5-7-5 structure

homework.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.67): research one vocation on msde.gov.in and note reasons for choice and social benefit

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly connects the chapter's celebration of vocations — craftspersons, boatmen, cooks, masons — to the idea of making vocations visible in public contexts. This framing links the poem's theme to the two practical tasks that follow.

Students complete the Career Mela poster task (p.64) independently: filling all template fields — event name, purpose statement, date and time, venue, highlights (streams, counsellors, interactive sessions), slogan, entry details, sponsors, issuing authority. Teacher circulates and checks that the functional register (public announcement, formal layout) is maintained.

Teacher introduces the Haiku form (p.67–68): 17 syllables, 5-7-5 structure, the Stevenson example on the board. Students compose one Haiku celebrating any vocation from the poem or their own lives. Two or three volunteers share with the class; teacher draws the parallel between the poem's compressed vocation-images and the Haiku's compressed form.

Closing synthesis: teacher reads aloud the poem's final line — 'The voice of their vocation is the voice of their identity. I hear Bharat celebrating, the varied voices I hear!' — and invites students to name, in one word each, what this chapter gave them about work, identity, and language. The MSDE research task is set as an independent exploration to be done outside class.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the chapter's entire arc — the democratic celebration of vocations in the poem, the functional form of public communication (the poster), and the compression of poetic form (the Haiku). The Haiku task builds directly on the poem's own technique of representing a vocation in a single sensory image, so students can use the poem as a model without reproducing it.
materials: Chalkboard for Haiku syllable count model
Notebooks for poster and Haiku drafts

items.source_section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
items.source_lo: Student analyses a poem's form, literary devices, speaker stance, and symbolic meaning using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A free-verse celebratory catalogue poem honouring Indian craftspersons, boatmen, electricians, cooks, and masons as bearers of national identity.
items.item_stem: Read the stanza on p.58 beginning “The carpenters celebrating”. Which of the following best describes how the poet conveys the carpenter’s skill in that line?

options.label: A
options.text: By comparing the carpenter to a musician who performs precisely.

options.label: B
options.text: By noting that the carpenter uses mathematical precision to create anything from wood.

options.label: C
options.text: By describing the carpenter singing while at work.

options.label: D
options.text: By stating that the carpenter brightens lives with cables and tools.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be conflating the musician/artisan-with-lutes line with the carpenter line.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may be misreading the boatman's singing line and attributing it to the carpenter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may be blending the electrician line about cables with the carpenter.

items.source_section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
items.source_lo: Student analyses a poem's form, literary devices, speaker stance, and symbolic meaning using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A free-verse celebratory catalogue poem honouring Indian craftspersons, boatmen, electricians, cooks, and masons as bearers of national identity.
items.item_stem:
Read the stanza on p.58 beginning “The boatmen gathering their nets”.

1. What does the boatman’s act of “sailing and singing while at work” suggest about the relationship between labour and identity in this poem?
2. The poet writes that the boatmen “return to tell the tales of life at sea.” Analyse how this detail extends the poem’s central claim that a vocation is also a voice.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the stanza on p.58 beginning “The boatmen gathering their nets from the shore.”

expected_elements: Sub-question 1: singing while working shows labour as joyful self-expression, not burden.
Sub-question 1: connects individual activity to the poem’s theme of vocational pride and identity.
Sub-question 2: ‘tales of life at sea’ transforms lived work experience into shared narrative.
Sub-question 2: links to the poem’s line ‘the voice of their vocation is the voice of their identity.’
Both sub-questions grounded in textual evidence from the poem.

items.source_section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
items.source_lo: Student demonstrates focused listening comprehension and inference by responding to a spoken conversation about real-world occupations.
items.source_context: Two friends discussing their parents’ occupations — a factory line supervisor and an automobile mechanic — and what drives curiosity about tools.
items.item_stem: Listen to the conversation between the two friends. Which statement about the girl is TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: She feels unsure about visiting her mother at the factory.

options.label: B
options.text: She is happy about delivering her mother’s lunch to the factory.

options.label: C
options.text: She is boastful about her mother’s job as a supervisor.

options.label: D
options.text: She already knows a lot about the tools used in the mechanic’s workshop.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have confused the girl’s straightforward happiness with hesitation, mishearing tone.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have over-read her mention of her mother’s role as boastfulness rather than matter-of-fact sharing.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have attributed the boy’s knowledge of tools to the girl instead.

items.source_section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
items.source_lo: Student demonstrates focused listening comprehension and inference by responding to a spoken conversation about real-world occupations.
items.source_context: Two friends discussing their parents’ occupations — a factory line supervisor and an automobile mechanic — and what drives curiosity about tools.
items.item_stem: After listening to the conversation, answer in two or three sentences: What does the boy’s habit of reading tool manuals tell us about how curiosity shapes the way a person engages with a vocation? Use details from the conversation to support your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The boy reads the manuals to understand the details of the tools his father uses, showing that curiosity moves beyond observation to active inquiry. This habit mirrors the way the girl’s mother supervises quality at the factory — both involve purposeful, informed engagement with one’s work rather than mere routine.

items.source_section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
items.source_lo: Student delivers an organised oral presentation taking on a vocational identity, articulating experience, challenges, and a message for a peer audience.
items.source_context: Students adopting the voice of a poem-vocation — carpenter, boatman, shoemaker, electrician, or cook — and speaking for peers.
items.item_stem: Choose any one of the vocations celebrated in the poem — the carpenter, the electrician, the boatman, the shoemaker, or the cook. Speak for one to two minutes as that person: introduce yourself, describe one part of your daily work, name one challenge you face, and end with a message you would share with your classmates.

expected_elements: Clear self-introduction naming the vocation and its core activity.
Specific, concrete description of one aspect of daily work.
Honest articulation of a real challenge associated with that vocation.
A closing message that connects personal pride to broader social value.
Spoken in coherent sentences with audible clarity and appropriate pace.

items.source_section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
items.source_lo: Student delivers an organised oral presentation taking on a vocational identity, articulating experience, challenges, and a message for a peer audience.
items.source_context: Students adopting the voice of a poem-vocation — carpenter, boatman, shoemaker, electrician, or cook — and speaking for peers.
items.item_stem: The poem claims that 'the voice of their vocation is the voice of their identity.' Do you agree that a person’s occupation shapes who they are, or do you believe identity is formed by other things? Argue your position clearly, giving at least two reasons with evidence from the poem or from life, and acknowledge one reason someone might disagree with you.

expected_elements: A clear, stated position (agree or disagree) on vocation as identity.
At least two reasons supported by evidence from the poem or real life.
Acknowledgement and engagement with a counter-argument.
Logical organisation: claim, evidence, counter-position, rebuttal.
Confident spoken delivery with appropriate register for reasoned argument.

items.source_section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
items.source_lo: Student produces a complete functional public document in an appropriate register using a real-life communicative scenario as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Designing a public awareness event that highlights diverse skilled occupations and their value to young people.
items.item_stem: Your school’s Students’ Council is planning a ‘Skill Spotlight Week’ to invite local craftspersons — a potter, a weaver, and a carpenter — to demonstrate their work to students. Design a notice to be displayed on the school notice board. Your notice must include: the name of the organising body, the event name and its purpose, the date and venue, at least two activity highlights, and a line encouraging student participation.

expected_elements: Correct notice format: heading, organiser, date, venue, body, sign-off.
Purpose clearly stated — awareness of craft vocations for students.
At least two specific activity highlights (e.g. live demonstration, Q&A).
A motivating closing line addressed to students.
Formal register maintained throughout with no conversational slippage.

items.source_section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
items.source_lo: Student produces a complete functional public document in an appropriate register using a real-life communicative scenario as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Designing a public awareness event that highlights diverse skilled occupations and their value to young people.
items.item_stem: A local newspaper has published an article arguing that vocational trades like pottery, carpentry, and weaving are becoming obsolete and should not be encouraged as career choices for young people. Write a letter to the editor, in 150–180 words, disagreeing with this view. Use the poem’s perspective on the dignity and cultural value of skilled vocations to support your argument.

expected_elements: Formal letter-to-editor format: address, salutation, body paragraphs, sign-off.
Clear counter-argument: vocational trades carry cultural and economic dignity.
At least one textual or contextual reference to the poem’s vision of vocation as identity.
Reasoned rebuttal of the ‘obsolete’ claim with a specific supporting point.
Appropriate formal register, accurate paragraphing, and word limit observed.

items.item_stem: Match each vocation in Column A with its correct description in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
|---|---|
| Sericulturist | A person who makes or sells sweets and chocolates |
| Horticulturist | A metalworker who fuses materials together |
| Confectioner | A producer of raw silk |
| Welder | A person who studies or grows garden plants |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Sericulturist–confectioner, horticulturist–welder; see answer_key for correct pairs.

answer_key.right: A person who studies or grows garden plants
A person who makes or sells sweets and chocolates
A metalworker who fuses materials together

items.source_lo: Student distinguishes precise domain vocabulary and identifies non-synonyms, demonstrating command of word meaning in context using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Vocation-specific terms (horticulturist, sericulturist, welder, confectioner) and synonym discrimination for words drawn from the poem’s diction.
items.item_stem:
Each sentence below uses a word from the poem — ‘myriad’, ‘hues’, or ‘precision’. Rewrite each sentence replacing that word with a synonym that fits the context, then write one sentence explaining why the word you chose is a better or weaker fit than the original.

1. The craftsperson worked with myriad (myriad) tools to complete the sculpture.
2. The weavers dyed the silk in hues (hues) of gold and blue.
3. The carpenter measured the wood with great precision (precision).

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable synonyms include: myriad — numerous / innumerable / countless; hues — shades / tints / colours; precision — exactness / accuracy / correctness. Students must then give one sentence justifying their synonym choice in context — e.g. 'numerous' fits because it emphasises countable variety, while 'innumerable' may overstate for physical tools.

items.source_section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
items.source_lo: Student creates an original compressed poetic form and undertakes comparative multilingual exploration of vocation-themed verse using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Composing a Haiku celebrating a chosen occupation and comparing the poem’s celebratory vision with R.L. Stevenson’s 'The Lamplighter'.
items.item_stem: Compose an original Haiku (5-7-5 syllables, three lines) that celebrates any one vocation — either one named in the poem or one from your own community. After your Haiku, write two sentences explaining which image or device from the poem you drew on for inspiration and why you chose that vocation.

expected_elements: Haiku follows 5-7-5 syllable structure exactly across three lines.
A specific vocation named and made vivid through a concrete sensory image.
Two sentences naming a device or image from the poem as inspiration (e.g. auditory imagery, personification).
Explanation of the vocation choice connecting to the poem’s theme of identity.
Language is compressed, precise, and avoids abstract statements.

items.source_section_title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
items.source_lo: Student creates an original compressed poetic form and undertakes comparative multilingual exploration of vocation-themed verse using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Composing a Haiku celebrating a chosen occupation and comparing the poem’s celebratory vision with R.L. Stevenson’s 'The Lamplighter'.
items.item_stem: The poem ‘Gifts of Grace’ and R.L. Stevenson’s ‘The Lamplighter’ (pp.67–68) both celebrate a working person through the eyes of an admiring observer. Design a brief comparative study (a single A4 page) that: (a) identifies one common device both poems use to honour the worker, (b) describes one important difference in tone or perspective between the two poems, and (c) explains which poem’s approach you find more effective and why. Present your study as a clearly organised written response with section headings.

expected_elements: One shared device accurately identified (e.g. auditory imagery, admiring speaker-observer).
One clear tonal or perspectival difference noted with textual evidence from both poems.
A reasoned evaluative judgment on effectiveness, not merely personal preference.
Section headings used; response is organised and within one A4 page.
Both poems named and their specific lines or images cited as evidence.
